name: Cuneus Equitum Stablesianorum

abilities.name: Wedge
abilities.text: The unit moves into a wedge-shaped attack formation.

attributes.name: Disciplined
attributes.text: This unit does not suffer a morale penalty when the general dies. It can also rally after routing more often.

attributes.name: Hide (forest)
attributes.text: This unit can hide in forests until enemy units get too close.

attributes.name: Immune to Fear
attributes.text: This unit is immune to the fear effects of scary units.

short: Stablesiani - the origin and meaning of this name remain unclear. Hoffmann suggests that these units were formed from stablemen, who, he hypothesizes, were originally attached to the new cavalry vexillations created under Gallienus. In a similar way, Speidel had previously claimed that the equites stablesiani were formed from stratores, soldiers who were attached to the personal staffs of provincial governors as stablemen or bodyguards. More recently, Speidel, rejecting this thesis, has suggested that the designation of stablesiani was originally applied to those cavalry units stationed in northwestern Italy during the reign of Gallienus under the command of Aureolus, who is identified as stabulensis, the senior officer in charge of the imperial stables. Although the origin of their title is disputed, the stablesiani appear to have been part of the comitatus (the field army accompanying the Emperor) during the military crisis of the 260-270s. Later, probably during the Tetrarchy and/or the reign of Constantine I, most of these units were permanently assigned to the garrisons of the frontier provinces. The existence of some of the equites stablesiani is testified up to the 6th century.
history: One of the simplest forms of one-armed catapult, the onager relied on twisted skeins of animal sinew which provided the power to hurl either rocks or shot. Inaccurate but powerful, it was an effective siege machine against buildings and fortifications, but was of far less use on the battlefield unless firing into massed infantry ranks. First mentioned by Philon of Byzantium in his treatise on ‘Mechanics’, the onager made use of a sling-like cradle attached to a firing arm. This arm was inserted, twisted, and propelled rocks or shot through torsion. As the firing arm was released, the sling-like cradle would unhook, firing the projectile. A padded beam was incorporated into the housing frame to restrain the arm. Larger machines could require as many as eight or ten crewmen, and the incredible recoil meant that they could not be easily or safely mounted on walls or towers. Quickly constructed wherever wood was readily available, onagers soon became a staple of ancient siege warfare.
strengths: Very low damage and armour penetration
